b: Definition: Uncommon, usually self-limited hypersensitivity disorder triggered by infections or drugs.
Infections: herpes simplex (most common), Mycoplasma, some fungi
Drugs: sulfonamides, penicillin, salicylates, hydantoins, antimalarials
Skin-homing cytotoxic T cells attack basal cells of skin and mucosae
These cells display antigens that cross-react with the inciting drug or microbe

qs.q: In the context of Erythema Multiforme, which clinical presentation is associated with the most severe, life-threatening outcome involving large areas of epidermal sloughing?
qs.e: Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) is the severe form of Erythema Multiforme where necrosis extends through the full thickness of the epidermis, leading to sloughing, fluid loss, and high mortality. Infection-associated forms are generally less severe.

qs.q: In the histology of Erythema Multiforme, what is the characteristic finding in the later stages of the disease?
o: Necrosis of basal epidermis with blistering
qs.e: Later stages of Erythema Multiforme show discrete or confluent zones of basal epidermal necrosis and blister formation. Subcorneal pustules are seen in impetigo, and psoriasiform hyperplasia in Candida.

exam: What bedside clues differentiate EM from urticaria? — Look for target lesions with three zones and fixed location >24 h; urticaria wheals are transient and lack concentric rings.
A patient with target lesions and oral erosions is on sulfamethoxazole. What is your next step? — Stop the drug, start supportive care, and consider antiviral if HSV suspected.
How would you manage EM in a clinic without HSV PCR? — Treat empirically with acyclovir if HSV is most likely, monitor response, and educate on trigger avoidance.
What features would prompt you to suspect progression to Stevens‑Johnson syndrome? — Widespread epidermal detachment >30% BSA, positive Nikolsky sign, systemic toxicity.
Explain why systemic corticosteroids are controversial in EM. — Evidence for benefit is limited; they may increase infection risk and delay healing, so they are reserved for severe mucosal disease.
A child presents with target lesions after a malaria episode treated with chloroquine. What is the likely cause? — Drug‑induced EM; stop chloroquine and provide symptomatic care.
Why is eosinophilia not a reliable marker for drug‑induced EM? — Eosinophil rise is variable and may be absent; diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and drug exposure timing.
What preventive measure reduces recurrent HSV‑triggered EM? — Daily suppressive acyclovir therapy in patients with frequent HSV reactivations.
ai.title: Erythema Multiforme
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Erythema multiforme (EM) is an acute, immune‑mediated hypersensitivity reaction producing characteristic target lesions, most often after HSV infection or certain drugs. It is usually self‑limited but can progress to severe mucosal involvement requiring urgent care.

b: Target lesion: central dusky area, surrounding pale edematous ring, outer erythematous halo
Typical sites: palms, soles, dorsal hands, forearms, face
Mucosal involvement in EM major; absent or minimal in EM minor
sections.p: EM is a self‑limited, immune‑mediated skin reaction presenting with target or iris lesions, often on acral sites. Diagnosis is clinical, based on morphology and distribution.

b: EM minor: <10% body surface, no or mild mucosal disease
EM major: >10% BSA or significant mucosal erosions
Progression to SJS: widespread epidermal detachment >30% BSA
sections.p: Two main categories are used: EM minor (skin only) and EM major (skin plus ≥1 mucosal site). Stevens‑Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a distinct, more severe spectrum.

b: HSV‑1 reactivation (most frequent)
Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
Sulfonamides, penicillins, antimalarials, NSAIDs
Traditional herbal remedies (possible allergens)
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the most common triggers are infections, especially herpes simplex virus (HSV) and Mycoplasma pneumoniae, followed by drugs frequently used locally.

b: Prodrome: low‑grade fever, sore throat, malaise
Lesions: 0.5–2 cm, round, with three concentric zones
Mucosal lesions: painful erosions on oral, genital, ocular surfaces in EM major
sections.p: Patients notice sudden appearance of symmetric, erythematous papules that evolve into target lesions over 24‑48 h, often preceded by a prodrome of fever or malaise.
Testing aims to identify the trigger and exclude mimics; many investigations are unavailable in low‑resource hospitals, so clinical judgment is paramount.

t.a: HSV PCR or culture from lesion swab
t.b: Is HSV the trigger? Positive result supports antiviral therapy
Is Mycoplasma involved? Positive IgM suggests recent infection
Is there eosinophilia or leukocytosis suggesting drug reaction? Elevated eosinophils support drug etiology
Does histology show necrotic keratinocytes and interface dermatitis? Confirms EM and rules out bullous pemphigoid

b: Rapid spread to >10% BSA
Severe mucosal involvement causing dehydration or airway compromise
Secondary bacterial infection of lesions
Progression to Stevens‑Johnson syndrome
sections.p: Although EM is usually benign, certain features demand urgent escalation.

b: Antiviral (acyclovir) if HSV trigger confirmed or strongly suspected
Stop suspected drug; avoid sulfonamides, penicillins, NSAIDs if implicated
Topical corticosteroid ointment for symptomatic relief
Oral antihistamines for pruritus
Adequate hydration and analgesia (paracetamol)
Wound care: gentle cleaning, non‑adhesive dressings
sections.p: Treat the inciting cause, provide symptomatic care, and monitor for complications. In low‑resource settings, supportive measures are often the mainstay.

b: Educate on HSV suppression (e.g., prophylactic acyclovir in recurrent cases)
Advise avoidance of identified drug class
Schedule review for mucosal healing and scar assessment
sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 1‑2 weeks; educate patients on trigger avoidance and early recognition of recurrence.

b: Erythema marginatum (rheumatic fever) – evanescent, non‑target lesions
Urticaria – fleeting wheals, no concentric zones
Fixed drug eruption – solitary, round, often on genitals
Stevens‑Johnson syndrome – extensive epidermal detachment, higher mortality
sections.p: Several dermatologic conditions mimic EM lesions.

b: Negative HSV PCR does not rule out HSV trigger (sampling error)
Normal eosinophil count can occur despite drug reaction
Mild leukocytosis may be from concurrent infection, not EM itself
sections.p: Laboratory and clinical findings may be non‑specific.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid expansion of lesions >10% body surface
Severe oral or ocular involvement impairing eating or vision
Signs of secondary infection: increasing pain, pus, fever
